items.name: The borrowed kettle (Freud)
items.passage: A man borrowed a copper kettle from his neighbour. When he gave it back, the neighbour complained that the kettle now had a hole in it. The man defended himself with three arguments. First, he had returned the kettle undamaged. Second, the kettle already had a hole in it when he borrowed it. Third, he had never borrowed the kettle at all.
items.question: Which statement best describes the reasoning in this passage?

options.B: The three arguments support one another, so taken together they make the defence much stronger.

options.D: The defence is valid, because the neighbour cannot prove exactly when the hole appeared.
options.E: None of the statements above gives a correct description of the reasoning in this passage.

items.why: Each excuse alone could clear the man, but they are mutually exclusive: he cannot have both returned it undamaged and never borrowed it. This joke is the origin of the term 'kettle logic'.
items.context: Freud tells this joke in The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) and in Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious (1905). He uses it to show how a dream can offer several mutually exclusive excuses at once because each one expresses the same wish.

items.context: Candide (1759) mocks the philosophy, associated with Leibniz, that this is 'the best of all possible worlds'. Pangloss's teaching appears in chapter 1, before the novel's disasters test it.
